news.title: Politics with Michelle Grattan: why Victoria’s unpredictable election matters nationally
news.text:
There are just seven weeks to go before the Victorian election on November 28. Labor is trying to beat the odds to do something it’s never achieved in the state before: after 12 years in power, it’s trying to win its fourth straight term.

But was Labor’s third change of premier this term – from Jacinta Allan to Ben Carroll in July – too late to make any difference? 

On today’s special election podcast, we’re joined by the Victorian premier, as well as Opposition Leader Jess Wilson and One Nation’s state Deputy Leader, Colleen Harkin.

The result is being closely watched around Australia, particularly as a test of One Nation’s strength. 

The election result remains surprisingly unpredictable, as Tony Barry – a former senior Liberal staffer turned director of polling and political consultancy firm Redbridge – explains.

Why it’s still too close to call

Barry said “there is a massive mood for change in Victoria”, with about 75% of Victorians saying the state is heading in the wrong direction.

Even after the leadership change from Allan to Carroll, Barry said there’s been no lift on Labor’s vote.

On a vote share basis, we have not picked up any improvement in Labor’s vote. That’s not to say that might [not] improve over the next seven weeks. But these decisions are always a risk versus reward proposition.

Jacinta Allan’s numbers were terminal. She was in the net –42 on personal favourability. To give you a sense of how bad that is, Donald Trump is net –59 in Australia […] Net –42 was catastrophic.

[…] I get the sense in focus groups that they’ve just moved on from the Labor party. It’s all too little, too late. It’s almost like, to use an analogy, like a divorcing couple and the husband at the last minute promises to make all these changes. And the wife’s not buying it. It’s that kind of vibe in the focus groups right now. 

But while “there’s very little love for the government and they’re polling at around 25% primary vote”, Barry said the Coalition will have to overcome Labor’s significant electoral buffer. 

The Labor government can afford to lose 11 seats, but they’ll still be a majority government. They’ll still have 45 seats – 45 being majority. So that gives them a lot of room to play around with.

Now, oppositions have won this sort of quantum of seats in the past. [The Liberals’] Jeff Kennett did when he first came to power. But the important thing to note when Jeffrey did it, he only needed about three or four seats to win majority. Campaigns are, at its core, an allocation of resources. They only had to really allocate resources to win three seats, and they won about 18, 19, from memory.

[…] So whilst I think all indications are Jess Wilson will be the next premier, with an 11 seat buffer, we wouldn’t write off Labor just yet.

Carroll: ‘it’s never been done before’

Victoria’s Premier, Ben Carroll, was only installed in late July, after his predecessor Allan abruptly resigned.

He’s dealing with a complicated Labor legacy, from COVID lockdowns, to high debt and allegations of Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU) corruption on Big Build projects – now the subject of a royal commission.

On state versus federal issues, Carroll said some national issues are having an impact on Labor’s support in Victoria.

Look, there’s no doubt that some of the federal government’s changes around housing and investment are resonating. There’s no doubt that the rising interest rates are resonating. 

Carroll admitted he’s behind at the moment, but declared “we’re coming home”.

It’s never been done before, a fourth election victory for Labor in Victoria. I believe we are behind, but we’re coming home: 121 new schools, 12 new hospitals, 100 level crossings removed. Best NAPLAN results. Highest paid nurses, highest paid teachers. Free dental. Bringing our road maintenance back in house. Integrity, law and order, financial responsibility. A strong state where workers and less fortunate are brought along. That’s the Labor way. 

He insisted he would “throw back the keys” rather than do a deal with the Greens to form minority government – and challenged the opposition to do the same rather than deal with One Nation.

I’m very clear. There’ll be no deals with the Greens. They are a party of protest.

 Read more:
 Ben Carroll is the new Victorian premier. He has a long and urgent to-do list – and 4 months until an election

Wilson: ‘repairing the budget is the most important thing’

Despite Labor’s uphill battle to hang onto power, that doesn’t guarantee an easy victory for Opposition Leader Jess Wilson. 

To win majority government, she will have to pick up 16 seats. Local memories are still fresh of Liberal Party instability, highlighted during the Moira Deeming saga. And Wilson is also under challenge from the rise of One Nation.

Wilson is currently shadow treasurer, as well as opposition leader. How long would that continue if she became premier?

The reason why I took on the role of shadow treasurer, and will continue to hold the role of treasurer in government, I’ve said that we will deliver a economic update within our first 100 days. And then thereafter look to hand over the portfolio of treasurer.

[…] Why I see [being treasurer as] so important in those initial days of government is because repairing the budget is the most important thing we can do in this state to deliver everything else that Victorians need. 

Wilson also forecast a shake-up to the Victorian public service.

It was the former ombudsman here in Victoria that spoke about the politicisation of the public service. And I think all Victorians have seen our public service grow over the past decade, and at the same time we have not seen our services improve here in Victoria. 

[…] We will make machinery of government changes to implement our agenda. But we’ve also announced a hiring freeze on back office public servants […] so that we can see the public service be recalibrated in its size to 2014-15 levels, adjusted for population growth, to reflect the fact that the public service here in Victoria has grown at 60% over the past decade, while population growth has only been 19%. 

Harkin: One Nation ‘will work with anybody to remove Labor’

Pollster Tony Barry noted Victoria has traditionally being One Nation’s weakest state, though its recent support in the polls has stayed “fairly consistent”. 

Even if there were campaign controversies, Barry said it was hard to see the party winning less than 15% of the vote statewide, predicting:

[One Nation] will come first or second in a few seats. But I don’t think it’s going to be as many as people think. I think they’ll perform better at a federal level. We’re yet to see how their campaign will play out, and campaigns still matter.

But One Nation’s Victorian Deputy Leader, Colleen Harkin, said her party wants to win government in its own right. 

Harkin, a one-time federal Liberal candidate, recently quit the Liberals after decades of membership to join Pauline Hanson’s party.

She said her values and attitudes hadn’t changed; instead, the Liberal Party had.

Over the years of being involved in the Liberal Party, I was increasingly concerned with their lack of commitment to core principles [… and] with their policy decisions. And it was really death by a thousand cuts. 

[…] It was actually my son who made a comment one night that I got off the phone from speaking on some policy thing, very frustrated. And he said to me, ‘I don’t know why you keep doing it, Mum, because you’ve been saying forever they don’t stand for anything you do’. And it took me a couple of weeks to process that. And I eventually sort of went, ‘you know, he’s right […] I haven’t changed, they have’.

She said One Nation was prepared to work with a minority Coalition government if need be, in exchange for policy outcomes.

We will work with anybody to remove the Labor government. Labor is our enemy, if you like that word, and the Coalition is our competitor. If they end up being in government, and needing our support, we would definitely have issues that we would be asking or demanding in return for confidence and supply. But our aim is to win ourselves.
news.summary: Premier Ben Carroll, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson, One Nation’s Colleen Harkin and pollster Tony Barry preview November 28’s closely watched election.

That manoeuvre, they argue, violates the separation of powers established in the US Constitution.

“The founders made clear more than 200 years ago that the executive can spend money only according to Congress’s direction,” Common Cause’s lawsuit said.

The two lawsuits also point to a provision Congress includes in its appropriation bills barring the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda purposes”.

Both complaints seek to have the ads to be declared illegal and for the expenditures to be stopped. They also pushed for steps to be taken to recover any money already spent on the ads.

The Democrats’ lawsuit was filed in Washington, DC, while the Common Cause complaint will be heard in the southern district of New York.

Trump has faced mounting criticism over the ads, which began airing in September.

So far, the advertising campaign has cost more than $12m to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.

The $20m Trump tapped for the ads comes from a $175m package Congress assigned to the Department of Homeland Security as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda.

Critics have pointed out that one of the ads appears nearly identical to a television spot Trump used in his re-election campaign in 2024.

Three ads have aired so far. In one, a choir sings “love me” over a montage of Trump as he declares the US will “never be a communist country”. Another uses images of Mount Rushmore as Trump heralds a new “golden age of America”.

The third is darker: Trump walks towards the camera in black and white, warning of a “final battle” against the “deep state” and other perceived enemies.

On Wednesday, the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos released a poll showing the ads are highly unpopular. Some 86 percent of the Americans surveyed, including four out of five Republicans, said it was inappropriate for Trump to have used public money for them.

Trump has defended the ads as “promotion for the country”, and he has argued they were similar to public outreach campaigns put out by previous administrations.

But after a bipartisan backlash, Trump said on Monday that he would start paying for future ads himself instead of using public funds.

He did not, however, commit to paying back the money already spent on the existing ads.

Members of Trump’s Republican Party have been among those speaking out against the ad campaign.

Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, said the advertisements resembled something former Hungarian leader Viktor Orban would put out.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, meanwhile, indicated he agreed with the message in one of the advertisements, but he emphasised that “it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars”.

news.title: The 'Gate of Tears' at the centre of Houthis' latest battle for control
news.text:
Within the past month, the Iranian-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have reignited a decades-long conflict.

At the heart of renewed fighting is control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key trading corridor better known as the Gate of Tears.

The Houthis stormed down Yemen's coast in September, seizing the port city of Mocha in a bid for power over the strait.

Now, Yemeni forces have recaptured the city in a major counteroffensive and deployed more than 100 fighter jets to guard the waterway.

But it is a fight that seems anywhere but over.

And one that could impact Australia's supply of everything, from T-shirts to medicine.

What is the Gate of Tears?

The Gate of Tears, or Bab el-Mandeb Strait, is a waterway at the southern end of the Red Sea — between Yemen, Djibouti and Eritrea.

Named for its precarious route, it lies on the opposite side of the peninsula to the Strait of Hormuz, the shipping corridor whose traffic has been dramatically affected as the US and Iran wrestle for its control.

The strait is 29 kilometres wide at its narrowest point, limiting traffic to two channels for inbound and outbound shipments.

The Yemeni island of Perim divides the path.

To the north lie the port cities of Hodeidah and Mocha.The cities, which the Houthis have seized, give a commanding view over approaching vessels.

On September 11, the group also seized the strategic Perim, where the United Arab Emirates — a former Saudi ally — had been building an air base.

Since then, a Saudi-backed counteroffensive has regained control of Mocha and attacked Houthi members in Hodeidah.

What is behind this latest conflict?

The Houthis' desire to control the strait extends beyond the Iran war.

The fight over key ports are part of a continuing civil war in Yemen, between the Houthis and a Saudi-backed government.

From 2015 to the 2022 truce, Saudi Arabia was involved in a combined air and limited ground campaign in Yemen, fighting against the Houthis, a group Australia lists as a terrorist organisation.

The fragile truce collapsed this year, after an air strike hit the Sana'a International Airport, preventing an Iranian flight carrying a Houthi delegation to land.

Houthis blamed the attack on a Saudi-led coalition, and responded with missile and drone strikes on Saudi Arabia, including one that targeted Riyadh.

They also targeted Saudi's oil infrastructure.

In July, the Houthis launched a maritime blockade on Saudi shipping tankers and territory in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The group had conducted a similar attack on commercial ships passing through the strait in 2023—2024, in response to Israel's invasion of the Gaza Strip.

However, this latest blockade exempted non-Saudi vessels.

Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthis' political bureau, told the Associated Press it wanted Saudi Arabia to lift a long-running blockade on the territory the group controls.

A Saudi counteroffensive has since seen the strait recaptured and tit-for-tat fighting escalate.

Both Saudi and Houthi officials have reported missile strikes and targeted attacks on major airports across Yemen and Saudi Arabia.

The renewed conflict has also seen more than 200,000 Yemenis flee their homes, according to UN estimates.

The United Nations estimated at least 150,000 people — including fighters and civilians — had been killed in Yemen's civil war, which began in 2015.

It had pushed about 5 million people to the "brink of famine".

How important is Bab el-Mandeb to trade?

It serves as the southern gateway to the Suez Canal, meaning ships must pass through it to access the canal from the south.

Before the Iran war in February, about 10-12 per cent of global trade passed through the waterway, Sanjoy Paul, an Associate Professor of Operations and Supply Chain Management at the University of Technology Sydney said.

"It has always been a critical route for shipping," he added.

In 2023, the strait handled approximately 9 per cent of global oil demand, according to the International Sustainable Development Observatory (ISDO).

And for Asia and Australia, the shipping lane is even more significant.

Oil, medicine, fertiliser, textiles, and machinery were all transported through that route, Dr Paul said.

When it was a choke point, ships had to travel around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope which could take three times as long.

"This additional time increases shipping time, increases cost of transportation, increases insurance as well," Dr Paul said.

For customers, that meant shortages and price surges.

Following the Iran war and a battle over the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait became a "lifeline", Dr Paul said.

Saudi Arabia had built an East-West Pipeline to divert crude oil flows through the Red Sea path

As of June, 3.42 million barrels of Saudi oil flowed through the strait, according to Kpler data.

"This became the alternative route," Dr Paul said.

What does this mean for Australia?

US President Donald Trump has been hesitant so far to become involved in this latest conflict, saying the Houthis "don't want to fight with us".

 "They would much prefer not having us involved, and they're letting most ships go through," he told reporters in late September.

But Qatar has warned the world cannot "afford" for the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to close.

"The whole world is going to suffer and it's going to be catastrophic for the entire world," Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman, said.

Saudi Arabia exports about 70 per-cent of the global oil supply, and most of its buyers are Asian nations who sell onto Australia.

If the fight for control was to escalate, it might lead to a particularly "devastating impact" on Australia's oil supply, Dr Paul said.

He said a further blockade would be "another blow to shipping and transportation", in addition to decreased use of the Strait of Hormuz.

"That increased demand at a global level will again translate into higher prices," Dr Paul added, about the impact on Australian fuel.

While a chokehold may hit consumer pockets, Dr Paul was concerned about Australia's access to critical supplies, such as medicine.

"It could be another important consideration: How in Australia we can prepare to stock key medicine?" Dr Paul said.

"Because those sort of things will be impacted for a long time.

"We may need to rethink our medical situation, how we can have enough stock here.
news.summary: The Bab el-Mandeb Strait has become a "lifeline" for global trade. But in the battle between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and the Houthis, it's even more important.
news.author: Tessa Flemming

news.title: Trump promises to prevent destruction of San Diego, Los Angeles
news.text:
WASHINGTON, October 8. /TASS/. The White House will not allow the American cities of San Diego and Los Angeles to be destroyed as a result of the conflict between Washington and Tehran, US President Donald Trump stated.

The president had already spoken on Monday about the possibility of destroying these two cities. However, he did not elaborate on his remarks. White House Communications Director Steven Cheung later stated that Trump was referring to a potential threat to American cities if the US did not take military action against Iran over Tehran’s nuclear program.

The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, in the early morning hours of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached on the Strait of Hormuz. Nearly 25% of the global oil trade and about 20% of the liquefied natural gas trade pass through the strait. The US administration then effectively signaled that it would cease the use of large-scale military force against Iran and shift to attempting to economically strangle the country through sanctions.

news.text:

Global goods trade is withstanding the drags of tariffs, wars and geopolitical rifts, fueled by the boom in demand for artificial intelligence gear and staying resilient as the US and China rewire their economic dependencies, a new report showed.Growth in merchandise trade this year is forecast at 4.6%, stronger than the 3.6% gain predicted in January, according to the DHL Globalization Tracker, which is co-produced by the Bonn, Germany-based parcel delivery giant DHL Group and New York University’s Stern School of Business. The outlook for next year was upgraded, too, to 3.6% from a January projection of 2.7%.Gloomy forecasts heading into 2026 driven by US President Donald Trump’s demolition of the rules-based trading system have proved off target, and separate figures from the CPB Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis confirmed last month that trade volumes worldwide hit an all-time high in July. Almost three-quarters of cross-border commerce is still conducted under the World Trade Organization’s low-tariff terms.The DHL-Stern report, released Wednesday, sees annual goods trade growth averaging 3.45% through 2029 — compared with 2.7% a year over the past decade — though the pace slows over the next three years.“Partners may be changing within the top trading economies, but trade has still been occurring and adjusting to a ‘new normal,’” WTO Deputy Director-General Jennifer Nordquist, who served on the Council of Economic Advisers during Trump’s first term, said last week at a conference in Switzerland. “One man’s protectionism may be another’s economic security.”Live EventsBloombergTrade growth typically tracks the ups and downs of global GDP, but lately the flows of exports and imports have held up better than broad economic activity. Shipping gateways in China have recently struggled with congestion, adding delays and pushing up container rates. The Port of Los Angeles, the largest in the US, had its busiest June-to-August stretch on record.Trump’s policy unpredictability and the need to pad inventories against sudden White House changes are among the reasons for the durability of demand, but AI is the main driver of the current freight boom, according to the DHL-Stern report.AI-enabling goods accounted for 42% of all merchandise trade growth last year, a share that jumped to nearly 76% during the first quarter of 2026, the report said, citing WTO and OECD data.“I see trade flowing — there is demand, there is supply,” said Beat Simon, DP World’s group chief commercial officer and chief operating officer for logistics, in an interview Wednesday. “It’s not only the digital revolution. Underneath is an enormous physical supply chain.”That helps explain why shares of A.P. Moller-Maersk A/S, the largest publicly traded container carrier, climbed to a record this week, and the CEO of one of the world’s largest freight forwarders sees at least three years of double-digit growth in logistics services catering to tech giants and their data centers.China’s StrengthAI equipment exports have given a huge lift to Asian economies hit hard by higher fuel prices. A US government report released Tuesday showed American imports increased 57% from Taiwan through August this year, 44% from Vietnam and 28% from South Korea. Chinese imports into the US were down 16% from a year earlier.Still, in their report, NYU researchers Steven Altman and Caroline Bastian said China’s exports expanded even faster than the global average and are finding markets other than the US to sell to, raising concerns about unfair competition in economies such as the European Union.Plenty of supply and demand headwinds exist, though, and wars in Ukraine and Iran have had “severe but concentrated” effects on trade. Government policy is “another negative force,” the report said, even though the “global impact is more limited than the dramatic nature of the policy changes might suggest.”The US share of global imports was 13% in 2025, and about half of American imports were exempted from Trump’s higher tariffs, the report noted. “Despite the recent shocks to the international trade environment, the outlook for trade has actually improved,” it said.The DHL-Stern report assesses whether globalization in other forms — flows of capital, information and people — is retreating in a connectedness index where 0% equals no cross-border activity and 100% reflects no border or distance hindrances.Capital and information “recorded the largest increases in international relative to domestic activity in 2025,” helping push the overall index to a record high of 25.8% in 2025.That level “strongly challenges the notion that globalization has gone into reverse. news.title: Trump is giving ex-MLB star Roger Clemens the Medal of Freedom, saying the Hall of Fame has cheated him
news.text:
Donald Trump has announced that he will honor former MLB star Roger Clemens with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, saying that the Baseball Hall of Fame has cheated him. 

Trump listed Clemens' impressive stats at a rally in San Antonio, Texas, Wednesday night, where the one-time superstar pitcher introduced Trump to the stage. The president has been traveling to red states to boost GOP candidates’ chances in the midterm elections as Democrats gain ground. Clemens has been a vocal Trump supporter for several years. 

Clemens was a two-time World Series Champion with the New York Yankees and won seven Cy Young Awards, the highest honor for MLB pitchers, during his career. But he has also been mired in controversy over allegations of extramarital affairs and steroid use, which he has denied. 

Trump recalled playing a round of golf with Clemens, during which he said, “It's a ridiculous thing that you're not in the Hall of Fame with that kind of a record.”

The president then said, “Forget about the Hall of Fame,” and announced that he was going to give him the Medal of Freedom — the highest civilian honor.

Trump then welcomed Clemens back on stage, and the former baseball player told a crowd of the president’s supporters that he was “stunned.”

“This supersedes anything that obviously I've done in my playing career, and to get it from this man, this president, there wouldn't be another president I'd want to get it from,” Clemens, who is now based in Texas, said, adding that Trump was a “winner” too. 

“I can't thank you enough. That's a huge honor,” Clemens told the president. 

Clemens will join the likes of civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. and the Apollo 11 astronauts when he receives the Medal of Freedom. 

Trump’s announcement comes more than a decade after Clemens’ former trainer, Brian McNamee, claimed that he injected Clemens multiple times with steroids and human growth hormones from 1998 through 2001. 

It was also reported by the New York Daily News in 2008 that Clemens had a decade-long affair with the now-late country music star Mindy McCready. 

Clemens has been married to his wife, Debbie, since the 1980s, and they have four children together.
news.summary: Clemens is an accomplished baseball player, but he’s also been plagued with scandals, including allegations of steroid use

news.title: Fed Minutes Show Hawkish Unity Behind September Rate Hike
news.text: All 19 Federal Reserve officials backed the decision in September to raise interest rates, with many supporting the move to guard against the risk of intensifying inflation pressures.A separate group of officials said higher rates were necessary based on their outlook for the economy, signaling greater concern for elevated inflation, according to minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee Sept. 15-16 meeting released Wednesday in Washington."Most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end," the minutes said.FOMC voters unanimously backed the decision last month to raise the target range for their benchmark rate by a quarter-percentage point to 3.75% to 4% - the first increase since July 2023. The move came amid signs the broader economy was accelerating.ALSO READ: 'Calibrated' Turn Vs Off-Cycle Shocker: How The New RBI Hike Cycle Compares To 2022"Several participants commented that the underlying momentum in the economy appeared to have increased," the minutes also said.The record also revealed a discussion about financial conditions. Many officials commented that despite the recent rise in longer-term Treasury yields, "financial conditions appeared to be supportive of economic growth, with equity prices having risen substantially this year and spreads on corporate bonds having remained narrow."Chairman Kevin Warsh told reporters following the Sept. 16 decision the move was aimed at removing a "dose of accommodation" as inflation remained stubbornly high. His comments fueled market bets for another increase in October.The decision also prompted criticism from President Donald Trump, who blamed the rate increase on Warsh's colleagues, whom he claimed were being "very political."Since the meeting, however, a series of comments from key Fed officials have indicated the central bank may be in no rush to raise rates again.Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams said in separate speeches last week they believed the central bank has time to assess the economy before considering another rate increase. Investors promptly reeled in their expectations for a rate hike this month.Repricing ExpectationsInvestors on Wednesday were pricing in a roughly 20% chance of another quarter-point hike at the Fed's Oct. 27-28 meeting, down from around 70% in the days following the September decision, based on federal funds futures. news.title: We’ll be out of Iran soon; oil prices will come down like a rock, says Trump
news.text:
Washington, Oct 8 (SocialNews.XYZ) US President Donald Trump has said the war with Iran will end very soon and predicted a sharp fall in global oil prices once the conflict is over, while insisting that Tehran would never be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon.

Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, Trump defended the American military operation against Iran and said his administration was determined to eliminate the nuclear threat posed by Tehran.

"And just as I promised, I am ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. They will never. They know that," Trump told supporters.

He suggested that American involvement in the conflict was approaching its conclusion.

"And we'll be out of there soon, and you watch those oil prices come down like a rock and watch everything -- everything else is coming down," he said.

The President argued that previous administrations had failed to confront Iran's nuclear ambitions and that military action had become necessary.

"That should have been done by past presidents for many years. It should have been done, but nobody wanted to take it on," he said.

Trump acknowledged that the conflict had affected oil prices but maintained that the increase was smaller than many had anticipated.

He said some had expected prices to rise threefold, fourfold or even fivefold because of the military operation.

At a separate White House event, Trump repeated his prediction that the conflict would end soon.

"Oil will drop like a rock as soon as we're finished with the war, which will be very soon," he said.

"It's going to be very soon. One way or the other, we'll be finished with it," he added.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also linked rising borrowing costs and inflation to the conflict in the Middle East.

"What we are seeing is headline inflation is high because of the energy shock," Bessent said.

He argued that underlying inflation had eased and predicted that energy supplies would improve once the conflict ended.

"So once we get on the other side of this Iran conflict, energy markets are going to be well supplied, and we will move down towards the Fed's target and mortgage rates and the 10-year will come back down," he said.

Trump also referred to diplomatic contacts involving his special envoy, Steve Witkoff, who has been involved in negotiations concerning Iran.

"He's working on the Iran deal and doing very well," Trump said.

However, the President indicated that he remained reluctant to accept an agreement merely to bring the confrontation to an end.

"I think the deal isn't really something that I want to do, but they're willing to offer us anything to stop, and we definitely, they will never have a nuclear weapon," he said.

news.title: DNC sues Trump over taxpayer-funded ads promoting him
news.text:
WASHINGTON >> Democratic Party officials sued President Donald Trump today, seeking a court order blocking his administration from using taxpayer money to pay for election-related TV ads.

The lawsuit, filed by the Democratic National Committee in federal court in Washington, accused Trump of a “blatant violation of the statutory ban on the use of appropriations for ‘publicity or propaganda purposes.’”

Taxpayer-funded television ads glorifying Trump began airing in late September, sparking a bipartisan backlash.

In a post on his Truth Social site on Monday, Trump said he considered the ads to be “a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.” but that they would no longer be funded by taxpayers. The White House said this week his MAGA PAC would fund the ads.

The DNC, the main governing organization of the Democratic Party, said in its lawsuit that the ads continued to air after Trump’s comments.

“With less than 30 days remaining before the midterm election and millions of public dollars apportioned to pay for propaganda ads still unspent, the DNC has no choice but to take action in defense of free and fair elections,” the lawsuit stated.

The ads ran during football games as recently as Sunday and during other programming. The New York Times reported that Trump personally directed the White House budget director to use taxpayer money for the TV spots, citing sources.

One ad features Trump declaring that “America will never be a communist country” while a chorus repeats the words “love me.” Another combines images of Mount Rushmore with footage of Trump praising a “golden age of America.”

Another new ad recently has featured ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. A source briefed on the matter told Reuters the government-funded ads will end this week.

The White House said Trump’s political action committee will not reimburse taxpayers for the ads that have run to date.

The ads end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for by the U.S. government.

news.title: Polanski’s final pitch in Holborn by-election: I’ll keep Burnham honest
news.text:
LONDON — Zack Polanski promised to smash Britain’s two-party political system — but his campaign for a U.K. parliamentary seat has leaned heavily on the idea that he can keep the existing prime minister honest.

POLITICO analysis of the online battleground in the Holborn and St. Pancras by-election – which takes place Thursday — shows the Green leader has been pitching himself as a protest vote for Labour-backing constituents in the London seat, which has been held by Labour since its creation in 1983.

The party has spent nearly £5,000 pushing ads on Meta’s platforms, which include Facebook and Instagram, promising that a Green win would help “keep the government in check.”

In one campaign video, Polanski takes credit for a series of Labour U-turns on their “most unpopular policies” over the last 12 months. A victory in the seat, he claims, would add further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to listen to the Greens, rather than “Nigel Farage, Donald Trump, or their corporate donors.”

An additional £7,000 has been spent by the party promoting graphics of recent newspaper headlines it thinks demonstrate the influence it holds over Burnham’s Labour government — including a Guardian story flagging a possible delay on North Sea gas field decisions until after the by-election.

“When Zack Polanski speaks, Labour listens. That is the power of the leader of the Green Party,” the accompanying ad copy states.

Building Brand Zack

The by-election marks Polanski’s first attempt to win a seat in the House of Commons. 

The left-wing leader oversaw a rapid polling increase for the Greens after taking charge in September 2025, snatching a Labour safe seat in Gorton and Denton under former Labour Prime Minister Keir Starmer the following February.

But its polling momentum appears to have stalled since Labour switched to Burnham, and the party has also faced internal rows over anti-semitism.

The party has spent around £8,000 on targeted ads highlighting endorsements for Polanski from local residents, including former independent candidates and NHS workers.

And at least £500 of that has been spent promoting effusive praise of the Green leader from his own local hairdresser.

Alongside a picture of the pair hugging, barber Rami is quoted saying: “I’ve been cutting Zack’s hair for years. When you chat to him you can tell how much he really cares.”

A significant number of the showcased endorsements come from former Labour backers and members as Polanski seeks to convince voters that Burnham’s majority — and the mid-term timing of the contest — means they can register a protest vote in the symbolic seat previously held by Starmer.

One standalone advert features former Labour member Gopa, who says: “We all know there will still be a Labour government whoever wins, so I’m excited for a Green candidate who will listen to us and help push Labour to do better.”

Other endorsements include a Labour member of three decades who says she is now backing Polanski after her former party “lost its way and let me down.” Ex-Labour councillor Naser says he’s switched his allegiance to “keep the pressure on, and keep Labour in check.”

The Labour pitch

By contrast, Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali has kept her campaign local.

 She has spent more than £21,000 with Meta promoting dozens of slick cinematic clips and polished graphics pitching herself as a “local champion.” 

Supported by Labour’s well-oiled digital team, Abdi-Wali’s online campaign focuses heavily on her experience of arriving in the area as a child refugee, and her subsequent career as a local councillor.

Labour has also pumped more than £20,000 into Google’s ad program. The majority of that sum was spent on bitesize YouTube ads, with the remainder spent on buying up sponsored Google search results in an attempt to grab the attention of voters hunting for information about the contest.

Also running

Britain’s hard-right Restore Britain has also been making a pitch to voters in Holborn and St Pancras — while openly admitting it has no chance of winning in “one of the most left-wing seats in Britain.”

Rupert Lowe’s party has spent around £30,000 on Meta ads positioning itself as a “genuine patriotic alternative” to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK — which has not spent significant cash in the contest. 

Restore’s spending included £1,500 promoting a “quiz” comparing comments from Reform politicians with Restore’s more hard-line agenda. A further £2,000 went on promoting a graphic of the “ten reasons” why voters should support it.

That list includes removing “millions of foreign nationals who hate who we are,” a promise to “reverse the Islamification” of London, deport “foreign tramps who ruin our city” and force “healthy” benefit claimants to clean graffiti and pick litter.

In a further attempt to present his insurgent party as a credible alternative to Reform or the Conservatives, Lowe’s paid online content repeatedly describes the by-election as a “free hit” for right-wing voters to “vote with your heart.”

“They don’t want the capital reformed, or conserved,” one paid ad states. “They want London restored.”
news.summary: Zack Polanski leverages ex-Labour voters — and his barber — in his bid to snatch a seat from the governing party in Thursday’s by-election.

news.title: US Military Finalises Iran Strike Preparations As Donald Trump Weighs Pre-Election Timing
news.text:
The Pentagon instructed US Central Command several days ago to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran, US officials said. The directive did not include a specific date for launching strikes, and US President Donald Trump has not made any final decisions. However, US and Israeli sources indicate that an operation could occur before the US midterm elections, and possibly ahead of the Israeli general election scheduled a week earlier.

If major combat operations resume, they are expected to involve extensive air campaigns targeting Iranian energy infrastructure, military command hubs, and nuclear facilities. Resuming the military campaign within the next three to four weeks could influence the upcoming US midterms, particularly as escalating hostilities threaten to drive up global crude oil prices. RAF Fairford Base Threat Aimed To Kill US Troops and Destroy Military Aircraft, Says Official.

White House Maintains Strategic Flexibility

Defense and administrative officials emphasised that operational planning remains standard procedure while the commander-in-chief reviews his choices. "The Department's job is to develop and present military options to the President," a Pentagon official told . A White House official confirmed that Trump retains all tactical alternatives at any time.

"The US is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. Iran has been decimated, and things will go one of two ways: the easy way or the hard way," the official said. "President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States." US Evacuates Dozen B-1 Bombers From UK’s RAF Fairford Airbase Over Suspected Iranian Threat.

The disclosure comes after The Atlantic reported that Trump has been weighing whether to authorise renewed military strikes against Iran prior to election day.

Camp David Discussions and Stalled Negotiations

The operational momentum follows a high-level national security meeting at Camp David, where Trump and his senior advisers met for several hours to discuss foreign policy developments.

An Israeli official told Axios that a significant portion of the session focused on the potential resumption of large-scale military actions against Tehran. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said after the meeting that discussions centered on "long-term" foreign policy planning.

Concurrently, diplomatic tracks remain deadlocked. Qatari mediators continue to await an official response from Tehran regarding an American counterproposal that demands significant nuclear rollbacks.

"The discussion about possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran has increased. The chances of it happening before the elections is not high but we don't rule it out. After the midterms the chances of it happening increase significantly," a second Israeli official stated.

High-Level Coordination With Israel

Behind the scenes, President Trump held talks with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, marking their second phone conversation in recent days following weeks of minimal communication.

A US official said Trump and Netanyahu spoke about "remembrance and respect for the victims of the October 7 massacre." The discussion occurred shortly after Netanyahu held a strategy meeting with his national security team regarding Iranian developments. Netanyahu also spoke with Rubio earlier in the week.

Defense analysts expect that any renewed military engagement would see American and Israeli armed forces operating in close coordination. Israeli officials noted that the Iranian regime appears desperate and paranoid, creating risks that Tehran might attempt a preemptive strike to avoid facing a third surprise attack.

Domestic and Regional Political Ramifications

A resumption of open hostilities carries substantial political implications in both nations. A renewed exchange would likely trigger retaliatory ballistic missile barrages from Iran toward Israeli territory.

Within Israel, an active state of emergency or heightened conflict could alter campaign dynamics, potentially bolstering Netanyahu's standing and limiting opposition criticism in the closing stretch of the election cycle. In the United States, shifting energy markets and war footing could likewise reshape the broader electoral landscape heading into the midterm vote.

news.title: Trump Torched for Doubling Down on ‘Take Out’ LA or San Diego Comments in New Speech: ‘Disgusting and Dangerous’
news.text:
Donald Trump faced backlash Wednesday evening after seemingly doubling down on his “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego comment, with critics labeling the president’s remarks “disgusting and dangerous.”

Earlier on Wednesday, the president appeared at the Freeman Coliseum in San Antonio, Texas to support U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton and House candidate Carlos De La Cruz heading into the midterm elections. During his rally speech, Trump appeared to try a revised version of his “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego remark from earlier in the week, which had controversially been interpreted as a dare to Iran to attack the West Coast cities.

“We had no choice, because we can’t let them have a new weapon,” he said, addressing the reasons behind the war in Iran. “But you want to see trauma? You want to see problems? And I said it the other day: Let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way. Let them hit. You want to see a horror show? You want to see problems?”

He added: “Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles if you want to see some bad things happen. You want to see a country that would be in free fall?”

“We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country. We’re not letting that happen,” Trump assured, before indicating that Iran would use a nuclear weapon against the U.S. if given the chance.

While Trump appeared to reframe his prior remarks as a criticism of Iran, many online were taken aback by the president’s decision to touch on the topic again.

“Trump just said it again: Let Iran hit Los Angeles or San Diego,” the official X account for the Democratic Party wrote Wednesday evening. “Disgusting and dangerous. End the war and hold him accountable.”

Veteran journalist Jim Acosta expressed a similar sentiment, writing on X, “You can sanewash this all you want. This. Is. Not. Normal.”

Amy McGrath, a former Marine fighter pilot and political candidate from Kentucky, slammed Trump as a “lunatic” and highlighted how the U.S.S. Lincoln is slated to return to San Diego after a “grueling” deployment.

“What kind of lunatic talks like this? The USS Lincoln returns to San Diego tomorrow after a grueling 10+ month deployment. Sailors are finally coming home to their families,” she wrote on X. “And the President keeps saying, ‘Let them hit a missile into San Diego.’ What the hell is wrong with this man?”

On Monday, Trump touched on a similar topic while speaking to a rally crowd in Grand Island, Nebraska.

“They can take out a city,” Trump said of Iran. “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay. And it’s going to be over with very soon. It’s … almost over with – and they might keep going a little long. You know, they always say they have a big threshold for pain. They need it. Let me tell you. They need it. But it’s going to end very soon. And it will end one way or the other.”

Trump’s response team later clarified the president’s remarks, denying that he literally called on a foreign country to bomb U.S. cities. “You buffoons. He was saying the U.S. is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon — which they would if they had the chance,” Rapid Response 47 wrote on X Tuesday.

Yet, Trump’s statement sparked widespread controversy, prompting everyone from California Gov. Gavin Newsom and Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass to “The Gilded Age” star Carrie Coon to speak out. His Wednesday night remarks have sparked a similar reaction online.

news.title: Trump Texas Rally Takeaways as Paxton's Fate Hangs in the Balance
news.text: President Donald Trump told Texans to "pretend that I'm on the ballot" as he campaigned for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton in San Antonio on Wednesday night, using a high-profile rally to boost one of the GOP's most prominent candidates while touting his proposed $5,000 "Trump dividend" and awarding the Presidential Medal of Freedom to former MLB pitcher Roger Clemens. During his third visit to Texas in less than a month on Wednesday, Trump told Texans that Democrats would open the state's borders and ruin the economy, urging them to vote for Paxton and down-ballot Republicans. The president's show of support at Freeman Coliseum comes during the final weeks of a race that has drawn national attention because of its competitive polling, outsized $440 million spending and the controversial profile of the longtime Texas attorney general whose career has been shaped by legal and ethical controversies. Paxton remains one of Trump's most loyal allies, even as the president has faced investigations, litigation and impeachment proceedings. At a rally last week, Trump called Paxton a "pain in the ass," but he said this week that he doesn't regret endorsing him over incumbent Republican John Cornyn, who some pundits believed to be a safer choice. Trump Gave Paxton Unequivocal Endorsement Trump reassured the crowd that he remains fully behind Paxton, despite months of turbulence in the Senate race. Trump called Paxton "perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America" and said he was "probably the greatest attorney general in the history of the state of Texas." He also predicted Paxton would become "one of the best senators that we have in this country." He repeatedly urged supporters to vote for Paxton and framed the race as critical to preserving Texas' conservative identity. "We want good ol'-fashioned Texas values," Trump said. "If they get in, they will open your borders and let the entire world pour in." Paxton was brought on stage to make a one-minute remark about 80 minutes into the rally. He used the moment to praise Trump. "The thing I love about President Trump is he's here for us. He's here for Texas. He's here for America. He believes in this country. He's out fighting every day." Trump Turns Race Into a Referendum on Himself Trump asked supporters—as he has repeatedly during his red-state rallies—to "pretend that I'm on the ballot." He argued that Republicans perform better when he is on the ballot and urged Texans to vote as if the election were about him personally. He also touted his electoral history in Texas, saying Republicans had won the state "all three times" and claiming he had received more votes than any candidate in Texas history. Trump attempted to nationalize the contest and tie it directly to his own brand and said the country is in "the Golden Age of America." He reiterated his promise to give Americans $5,000 apiece if Republicans hold Congress. He said the checks would be sent within two days of victory. If Democrats win, he said, the country would enter a 1920s-type depression. He also touted that 20 million senior citizens will receive checks for $100 for Medicare reimbursements starting this week. "We're giving that money back to American seniors, as I promised," he said. Talarico Remains Target Trump devoted a substantial portion of his speech to attacking Talarico, repeatedly referring to him as "Talafreako." The president accused Talarico of supporting sanctuary cities, opposing border-wall construction, favoring criminal justice reforms, backing DEI initiatives, voting against anti-cartel measures and threatening Texas' oil and gas industry. He hurled insults at Talarico for being a vegan and wearing a mask. He told Texans that Talarico wants gun control. “He wants to take away and destroy your Second Amendment,” Trump said. Trump also said Paxton's opponent hasn't been seen in two weeks: "Where the hell is he?" Newsweek reached out to Talarico's campaign for comment during the rally. Immigration Remains the GOP's Closing Argument The loudest applause lines came when Trump discussed the border. He said the administration of former President Joe Biden allowed millions of migrants to enter the country and highlighted cartel violence, human trafficking and crime. He later played a lengthy border-focused video for the crowd. Trump repeatedly linked immigration to the U.S. Senate race by arguing that electing Paxton would help preserve the tougher border policies Republicans have championed in Texas. He brought in Marie Vega, whose son, U.S. Border Patrol Agent Javier "Harvey" Vega Jr., was fatally shot on August 3, 2014, by undocumented immigrants during a family fishing trip. She urged the crowd to vote Republican. Trump claimed that zero illegal immigrants have entered the country in 17 months. Trump Casts Texas as One Election Away From Becoming California The speech repeatedly returned to a familiar Trump argument: that Democratic victories lead to decline in the country. He described Democratic-run states as dirty, crime-ridden and dysfunctional, saying streets, sidewalks and even door knobs become "dirty" when Democrats take power. "When the blues get in, everything becomes dirty," Trump said. Trump argued that a Talarico victory would cause Texas to resemble California, New York and Illinois. "Texas will be almost instantaneously destroyed if Talafreako gets in," Trump said. Protesters Briefly Interrupt Rally Trump was interrupted by protesters several times. The crowd booed them and Trump dismissed them as "paid protesters," suggesting they were being funded by political opponents. "You know, many of these protesters are paid. You know that, right?" Trump said. "They're paid by enemies of our nation." In several cases, the protesters were escorted out and Trump returned to his speech. Roger Clemens Throws Out First Pitch Clemens, the former Red Sox, Yankees and Astros star pitcher who lives in Houston, introduced Trump. Clemens praised Trump for making the country "better," "stronger" and "safer," particularly on border security. He also called Trump "a damn good golfer" who has "gotten better with age." Trump recounted a golf game he played with Clemens, where he said he learned that Clemens hasn't been inducted into the Hall of Fame. "He's the greatest modern pitcher," Trump said. "He never admitted to anything. He's just a physical monster." He called on MLB to put Clemens in the Hall and presented him with the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Paxton vs. Talarico: Texas-Sized Spending While Texas was once viewed as a GOP stronghold, recent polling indicates that the Lone Star State is now a key battleground in the fight for congressional control. If successful, Talarico would be the first Democrat elected to statewide office in Texas since 1994. The Texas U.S. Senate race has already seen $440 million in spending, including nearly $175 million in outside funding, according to The Texas Tribune. Texas airwaves and digital platforms are saturated with ads attacking and defending both candidates. Paxton’s campaign told Politico this week that the Republican raised $18 million in July, August and September, more than double the $9 million raised in the second quarter. That's short of the $30 million Talarico's campaign reports raising from April through June, after bringing in $27 million in the first quarter. The Democrat’s campaign has not yet released figures for the third quarter, but the Tribune reported in September that Talarico has cumulatively raised $72 million since the start of 2025. The spending war has focused heavily on Paxton's record in office, while Republicans have sought to portray Talarico as aligned with national Democratic priorities. The sheer volume of resources devoted to the race has underscored how dramatically the political landscape in Texas has shifted compared with past election cycles, when many statewide Republican candidates faced little serious financial opposition. Paxton's Legal and Ethical Controversies Paxton entered the Senate race carrying years of legal and political baggage that have made him one of the most polarizing figures in Texas politics. Most notably, the Texas House impeached Paxton in 2023, accusing him of abusing the powers of his office. The impeachment centered on allegations involving a political donor and claims raised by former senior aides. The Texas Senate later acquitted him on all articles, allowing him to remain attorney general. The impeachment battle followed years of separate legal challenges, including a long-running securities fraud case that stemmed from allegations first brought before he became attorney general. Throughout those controversies, Paxton has consistently denied wrongdoing and argued that he has been targeted because of his conservative politics and willingness to challenge Democratic administrations in court. Supporters have embraced that argument and frequently point to his legal victories on immigration, election and federal regulatory issues. Critics, meanwhile, have argued that the various investigations and allegations raise broader questions about ethics and public trust. The debate over Paxton's record has become a central theme of the Senate campaign. Trump's Long Alliance With Paxton Trump and Paxton have maintained a close political relationship for years. Paxton became one of Trump's most visible allies following the 2020 election and drew national attention for his efforts to challenge election results in several battleground states. Trump repeatedly stood by Paxton during subsequent political battles and has continued to support him during the Senate campaign. Wednesday's rally represented the latest example of that alliance. That relationship has proved mutually beneficial politically. Paxton has remained popular among the Republican base that forms the foundation of Trump's support, while Trump's endorsements have helped cement Paxton's standing among conservative voters. The alliance has come under renewed scrutiny following reports that leaked audio captured Paxton discussing the political impact of Trump's presence on the campaign trail. Despite those reports, Trump has continued appearing alongside Paxton and urging Republicans to back him next month. news.summary: President Donald Trump came to Texas to campaign for Republican nominee Ken Paxton during the hotly contested Senate race.

news.title: Moment of Opportunity
news.text:
On 28 February, the United States and Israel shocked the world by launching strikes across Iran and assassinating the country’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Civilian casualties quickly mounted, including 150 civilians—mostly children—killed when American missiles struck an elementary school. Iran duly retaliated by targeting Israel and US bases across the region and throttling maritime transit through the Strait of Hormuz.

The unilateral aggression against Iran lacked international legitimacy and destabilised the entire Middle East. Arab countries suffered retaliatory attacks from Iran because they host American bases, and countries around the world faced high economic costs from spiking energy prices. The damage was also reputational for Gulf countries, in terms of safety and security.

Then, on 7 April, the New York Times published a detailed report about how Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had convinced US President Donald Trump to attack Iran, a decision that now needs to be examined from two perspectives.

First, it shows just how easily the US can be dragged into a war. Surely a nuclear-armed superpower should have extraordinarily robust decision-making mechanisms when it comes to matters of war and peace.

Second, it seems that the American victory in Venezuela caused the overconfidence that led to Iran. The Trump administration thought it was unstoppable with the use of military power. But things turned out to be much more complicated and difficult in Iran. By the time the Americans realised that the only similarity between the two countries was their oil reserves, it was too late. The image of America being stuck in a conflict with Iran is severely damaging. US adversaries used to be other superpowers like China and Russia, yet now Iran has joined the picture.

Meanwhile, Gulf countries have suffered as a result of American actions. Trust was already damaged in 2019, when the US failed to make good as a security guarantor following attacks on Saudi oil facilities. Now, US assets hosted by Gulf countries have become a vulnerability instead of a source of security. The US is no longer seen as a reliable security partner.

The Gulf countries will undoubtedly seek to diversify their partnerships—not only in defence but also in other areas such as trade—and this will further weaken US primacy in the region. China will likely be the biggest beneficiary, especially following its facilitation of Iranian-Saudi rapprochement in 2023.

Iran, despite all its losses, has proved that it can retaliate and resist American and Israeli attacks. The internal turmoil and regime change that many in the West expected did not happen. On the contrary, Iran defended itself while its people united in the face of the external aggressor.

That said, Iran must tread carefully. It should not mistake short-term advantages for long-term wins. Pride in defying more powerful adversaries could lead Iran’s leaders to pursue a maximalist approach in pressing their demands. But that would be counterproductive. Iran’s leadership must instead seize the moment and capitalise on what it has achieved.

Two major issues warrant closer examination: Iran’s internal political order and domestic welfare; and the broader regional order, which presents ample opportunities for mutually beneficial cooperation.

Even if it looks like Iran could sustain this conflict for much longer, Iranian leaders must consider the price of doing so. The primary responsibility of any government is to safeguard the welfare of the country’s people. With both the state and the people incurring heavy losses, the highest priority should be to secure sanctions relief and improve Iranians’ living conditions. Besides, the strategic leverage that Iran has gained over the Strait of Hormuz is not permanent. Alternative routes are being developed.

Iran’s leaders also must consider future relations with Gulf countries. Israel has long sought to push Saudi Arabia to join the US in confronting Iran, but the Kingdom has wisely refrained. Iran’s leaders should recognise this. They also must recognise that their reliance on regional proxies has not served them well. It has merely pushed Arab states toward Iran’s adversaries.

At a time when the Gulf countries are questioning their dependency on the US, continuing hostile action against them would only jeopardise Iran’s strategic gains and push Arab countries back into the old arrangements. For the region to reach a new balance, Iran and Saudi Arabia must normalise their ties. That alone would be a big step forward, because it would allow them to stop seeing each other as an enduring threat.

Moreover, regional normalisation between Muslim countries would in turn allow for progress on the Palestinian cause. Here, Iran must reckon with its own track record. Can it honestly say that its approach toward Palestine has helped? If anything, Iranian rhetoric has served as the pretext for Israel to do whatever it wants—and with unlimited military assistance from the US.

Iran must eschew a maximalist position. It can achieve sanctions relief, end the blockade, and progress toward reintegration into the international community, all without having to surrender. But the window of opportunity is closing. Following the US midterm elections in November, the Trump administration will feel less urgency to reach a deal. Indeed, it might even pursue revenge for the Republicans’ likely loss at the polls.

But just as Iran should move quickly before its negotiating position deteriorates, others should take its fears and threat perceptions into account. Decades of hostility toward the country have only hardened its position. The challenge for all sides is to reconcile the regime’s fears with Iranians’ right to prosper peacefully and safely.

news.title: Former aide says Trump knows a reckoning is coming
news.text:
It appears to be finally dawning on President Donald Trump that he will be catching more scrutiny after November if Democrats take the House and possibly the Senate, according to a former Trump media worker speaking with CNN.

On Wednesday Trump distanced himself from two of his top political advisers, writing that if their outside work [with Russia] presents a conflict, “I will terminate them, immediately!” 

Trump’s complaint came after The New York Times published a report showing James Blair, who now leads Trump’s outside political operation, and Chris LaCivita, Trump’s 2024 co-campaign manager, traveled to the Balkans last week for paid work on behalf of a pro-Putin government enclave. 

Trump claims he was unaware that the two men had traveled to the Balkans or that the two were representing a pro-Putin facet of the government until the New York Times piece, said sources speaking with CNN.

But Alyssa Farah Griffin, who worked in Trump’s first term as the White House director of strategic communications, told CNN anchor Anderson Cooper that the optics of this remained terrible.

“To frame either of these individuals is not senior … is laughable,” said Griffin. “These are very senior officials. LaCivita was important to his campaign. …[and] right now, 27 days from the midterms, his top political advisors are somewhere abroad and not working on maintaining the House.”

But even more telling, Griffin pointed to news of Trump saying he could have done “very bad things to Hillary Clinton” and others.

“I could have done very, very bad things to Joe Biden,” Trump said after he was asked what Democrats would impeach him for if the party wins back the House and the Senate in November. “I could have done very bad things to Barack Hussein Obama. I thought it was inappropriate to do so because you have to treat the office of the presidency with respect.”

But not so respected that he doesn’t target his other purported enemies, according to critics.

Trump was already impeached twice during his first term in office, one in response to a call he made to Ukrainian President Zelensky in which he pressured Ukraine to investigate Biden. He was later impeached following the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. In both cases, Republican allies in the Senate refused to impeach.

“Not helpful musings as your closing message heading into the midterms,” Griffin told Cooper. “It's been a preoccupation of the president's that he likes to remind people he didn't go after Hillary Clinton, but he could have. This is a common refrain that he goes back to. But this honestly feels like a bob in a weave as he's starting to process the fact that he's had total control of the White House and both chambers of commerce of Congress. And that's about to change.”

“He is going to be subject to oversight,” continued Griffin, speaking of incoming Democrats. “He remembers Impeachment 1. He remembers Impeachment 2, and I don't think he wants to deal with what comes with a potential Impeachment 3.”

news.title: Pro-Palestinian protesters turn on Mamdani, chant ‘traitor’ at Oct. 7 event
news.text: Small demonstrations, a message of support from U.S. President Donald Trump, sharp criticism from the top House Democrat and chants of “traitor” directed at New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani marked the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas massacre in the United States. Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform Wednesday: “Three years ago today, on October 7th, the World witnessed one of the darkest and most evil days in the history of Israel. Innocent men, women, and children were murdered, kidnapped, and subjected to unimaginable horrors at the hands of Hamas TERRORISTS.” “Today, we remember every innocent life taken, honor the survivors and their families, and remember the hostages who endured the unthinkable. I fought relentlessly to bring the hostages home, and reunite them with their loved ones, and I did, both the living and the dead!” “We will NEVER forget October 7th. We will NEVER forget the victims. And we will always stand against the forces of Terror and Evil,” Trump wrote. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, meanwhile, called for what he described as a “dramatic” change in U.S. policy in the Middle East. In a statement marking the anniversary, Jeffries condemned Israel’s actions in Gaza, saying the deaths of Palestinian civilians and the destruction in the territory were reprehensible and must not be allowed to happen again. He called on Washington to commit to the creation of a Palestinian state and work to end settler violence in the West Bank. At the same time, Jeffries stressed that the United States must remain committed to Israel’s right to exist, to removing Hamas from power and to combating terrorism. He also expressed solidarity with bereaved families and former hostages. Pro-Palestinian protesters turn on Mamdani Hundreds of pro-Palestinian demonstrators rallied across New York as the anniversary was commemorated, with protesters chanting slogans including “Long live Hamas,” “Death to the IDF” and calls to “keep the intifada alive,” while declaring that “resistance is justified.” Some demonstrators wore keffiyehs, carried Palestinian flags and displayed signs supporting Gaza and the Palestinians. At the same time, a gathering was held in Union Square billed as an evening of “quiet reflection and mourning” for those murdered on Oct. 7 and for the bloodshed that followed. The event was organized by Israelis for Peace. Pro-Palestinian demonstrators arrived and disrupted the ceremony, delaying it for several minutes. Participants at the vigil read out the names of Israelis murdered in the Hamas attack as well as Palestinians killed in Gaza. Mamdani also arrived at the Union Square event, where he was met by chants of “traitor, traitor, traitor.” The confrontation marked a striking reversal for a mayor who has long been closely associated with the Palestinian cause. Protesters accused Mamdani of retreating from promises he made on the issue before taking office and also demonstrated outside City Hall in Manhattan. In an interview with local news channel NY1 recorded before the vigil, Mamdani said: “We are talking about the third anniversary of a horrific war crime in which Hamas killed more than a thousand people and kidnapped hundreds more.” “We are also talking about the anniversary of the day when the Israeli government responded through what I describe as the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza, which continues to this day.” “The lesson for all of us is that humanity has to be something we believe in, in the fullest sense of the word,” Mamdani said. “We need to defend it, and we need to be able to call an atrocity what it is and fight for a future in which everyone is protected, no matter who they are or where they come from.” “As mayor, my job on Oct. 7, and my job every day, is to make sure that we keep people safe.” Mamdani also drew a distinction between criticism of Israel and antisemitism. “To be clear, I do not believe that every criticism of the Israeli government or of any prime minister is antisemitism,” he said. “What is unacceptable in this city are the acts of antisemitism that we have continued to see across the five boroughs. That is something we will never tolerate.”
news.summary: Trump vows the US will ‘always stand against terror and evil’ as top House Democrat Hakeem Jeffries calls for a dramatic policy shift and Palestinian state; New York mayor heckled at Union Square vigil

news.title: Democrats sue US President Trump over taxpayer-funded ad campaign  - St. Vincent Tribune – Daily St Vincent
news.text:
The Democratic National Committee has filed a lawsuit against United States President Donald Trump over television advertisements that were publicly funded and allegedly used to promote his political policies.

Ken Martin, who heads the Democratic Party’s leadership body, suggested in a statement on Wednesday that the ads were designed to bolster Republican odds in the upcoming November 3 midterm elections.

“Donald Trump is misusing millions of taxpayer dollars to fund pure propaganda ads in a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November,” Martin said.

A second lawsuit was filed later in the day over the same set of ads by Common Cause, a democracy watchdog group.

It argued that the ads were “overtly political” and therefore ran afoul of laws that bar public funds from being used for political propaganda.

“These ads are not public-service announcements,” Common Cause said in its lawsuit, citing a justification Trump has offered for the television spots. “They are personal publicity and political propaganda through and through.”

Both lawsuits argue that, to create the ad campaign, Trump directed the White House to repurpose $20m in funds that Congress allocated for commemorative activities related to border security, including for those killed in the line of duty.

That manoeuvre, they argue, violates the separation of powers established in the US Constitution.

“The founders made clear more than 200 years ago that the executive can spend money only according to Congress’s direction,” Common Cause’s lawsuit said.

The two lawsuits also point to a provision Congress includes in its appropriation bills barring the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda purposes”.

Both complaints seek to have the ads to be declared illegal and for the expenditures to be stopped. They also pushed for steps to be taken to recover any money already spent on the ads.

The Democrats’ lawsuit was filed in Washington, DC, while the Common Cause complaint will be heard in the southern district of New York.

Trump has faced mounting criticism over the ads, which began airing in September.

So far, the advertising campaign has cost more than $12m to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.

The $20m Trump tapped for the ads comes from a $175m package Congress assigned to the Department of Homeland Security as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda.

Critics have pointed out that one of the ads appears nearly identical to a television spot Trump used in his re-election campaign in 2024.

Three ads have aired so far. In one, a choir sings “love me” over a montage of Trump as he declares the US will “never be a communist country”. Another uses images of Mount Rushmore as Trump heralds a new “golden age of America”.

The third is darker: Trump walks towards the camera in black and white, warning of a “final battle” against the “deep state” and other perceived enemies.

On Wednesday, the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos released a poll showing the ads are highly unpopular. Some 86 percent of the Americans surveyed, including four out of five Republicans, said it was inappropriate for Trump to have used public money for them.

Trump has defended the ads as “promotion for the country”, and he has argued they were similar to public outreach campaigns put out by previous administrations.

But after a bipartisan backlash, Trump said on Monday that he would start paying for future ads himself instead of using public funds.

He did not, however, commit to paying back the money already spent on the existing ads.

Members of Trump’s Republican Party have been among those speaking out against the ad campaign.

Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, said the advertisements resembled something former Hungarian leader Viktor Orban would put out.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, meanwhile, indicated he agreed with the message in one of the advertisements, but he emphasised that “it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars”.

news.title: World News | US CENTCOM Rejects Iran's Claim of Hormuz Closure, Says 20 Million Barrels of Crude Moving Through
news.text:
Washington [US], October 8 (ANI): The US Central Command (CENTCOM) on Wednesday (local time) rejected Iran’s claim that the Strait of Hormuz is closed, saying commercial and energy traffic continues to move through the strategic waterway.

“CLAIM: Earlier today, a general from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed in media reports that ‘the Strait of Hormuz is closed’ and his country has ‘full control over it.’ This is FALSE,” CENTCOM said in a post on X.

“FACT: Traffic is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz right now carrying commercial goods and energy supplies, including 20 million barrels of crude oil. The United States and regional partners clearly control the strait,” it added.

https://x.com/CENTCOM/status/2107954036750119346
